Iowa Detonation Delayed
The US Army has
postponed the detonation
of roughly five tons of unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa from Friday to Monday, ahead of a temperature drop officials said could further destabilize the material. The two blasts are due to produce a dust cloud containing toxic lead particles that could travel up to 60 miles and impact thousands of people (
see map
A safety review of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in early 2026 revealed 68 barrels of
lead azide
degraded while in storage. The Army determined relocating the barrels would pose an unacceptable risk of an accidental explosion. The plan to detonate the barrels in underground concrete structures still raised concerns over potential soil and water contamination from airborne lead. Officials advised the approximately 360 residents of Middletown, Iowa, to evacuate their homes, with five days’ notice.
Lead exposure can impair brain development and lower cognitive ability. See a map of US communities with the highest risks of exposure
here
Myanmar Genocide Ruling
The International Court of Justice ruled yesterday that Myanmar
committed genocide
against its Rohingya Muslim minority, the first time the United Nations' highest court has held a country responsible for genocide in its 80-year history.
The case stems from a 2017
military crackdown
that killed an estimated 10,000 Rohingya and displaced over 700,000. Myanmar denies committing genocide, arguing its military was responding to insurgents. The case was brought in 2019 by the West African nation of Gambia, with 11 other countries later supporting it. In a 9-6 ruling, the court ordered Myanmar to investigate suspected perpetrators, facilitate refugees' safe return, and report on reparations within two years. ICJ decisions
are binding
but lack direct enforcement powers, leaving potential action to the UN Security Council, where China and Russia could block measures. The decision comes amid a pending genocide case against Israel over Gaza.
Read a Pulitzer Prize-winning
investigation

Greenland Deal Sealed
Denmark’s parliament unanimously
ratified
a deal with Greenland and the US yesterday aimed at strengthening North Atlantic and Arctic security. The trilateral agreement allows the US to expand its military presence in Greenland
while preserving the island as a semiautonomous Danish territory.
The US maintains one military base in northwestern Greenland,
Pituffik Space Base
. Established during the Cold War, it houses approximately 150 to 200 service members responsible for missile operations and space surveillance. The deal allows the US to expand the installation and establish additional bases across the island. President Donald Trump has also proposed building a "Golden Dome," inspired by Israel's
missile defense system
, to defend against potential long-range attacks amid increased Chinese and Russian naval activity in the Arctic. Greenland is the shortest flight path between Russia and the US.
Separately, melting sea ice is making Greenland's vast deposits of rare earth minerals, oil, and natural gas more accessible (
scroll for map
). These resources are critical to advanced defense, batteries, and energy technology.
